How TargetSage works, one module at a time

Run the agent that writes a gene’s evidence profile, train the reasoning policy with GRPO, then set up the positive–unlabeled scorer. The toys run live in your browser with the paper’s formulas; boxes marked Paper quote the paper’s own numbers.

Before anything is learned, an LLM agent writes every gene a profile in plain text. It rewrites the gene’s numbers as statements, fetches what the numbers miss, and checks the result. Run its six tools on an example gene, then change the gene’s situation and watch the profile change.

    What the fact-checker found

    1 gene whose profile gave away its label: a PubMed abstract called it “FDA approved”. The sentence was removed.

    385 genes (2.0%) with statements that disagree across sources, such as different localizations. They are kept and flagged.

    Why plain text

    The structured features are fixed columns; a profile is just text. A new database can be added to the profile without changing the model that reads it.

    Appendix C; Table 5 lists the 15 databases behind the 482 features.

    A small language model reads each gene’s profile together with the task and writes a rationale plus scores for 23 attributes. Nobody labels good reasoning, so TargetSage rewards a rationale by what it does downstream: does the gene’s new reading make the target ranking better? Step through one GRPO update on a toy, then let it train.

    The policy’s typical score per step

    Rewards move only in the second or third decimal, because one gene shifts among 600. GRPO divides by the group’s spread, so what counts is which rollouts beat the other three. With the KL weight at 0 the policy runs to the extremes; the KL term holds it near the model it started from.

    Paper Policy: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with LoRA (rank 32), trained by GRPO straight from the instruct model, with no supervised reasoning traces. G = 4 rollouts per gene at temperature 0.8; learning rate 5 × 10−5; clipped surrogate objective with KL regularization; one RTX 3090. The reward averages Adjusted F1 over all 15 tasks, from frozen module-3 scorers fitted once before any RL update (Sec. 3.3, Appendix F).

    Module 3 turns the three views of a gene into one score, and it learns without ever calling an unlabeled gene a negative. It has four parts.

    A. Gated fusion: each gene gets its own mix of the three views

    hm = σ(Wm um + bm),  α = softmax(Wg [hbio; hattr; hemb]),  hfuse = Σm αm hm

    The 482 structured features, the 23 attribute scores and the 256-number rationale vector are each projected to 256 dimensions. A gate reads all three and outputs three weights that sum to 1. Drag the point in the triangle to choose a mix; the bars show how much each view contributes to each fused dimension.

    Paper How the views are combined, macro Adjusted F1 over 15 tasks (Table 7a)

    Paper Which views go in (Table 6). Untick a view to drop it.

    The 16-dimension vectors are toy stand-ins: a sparse structured view, a smooth attribute view and a noisy embedding view.

    B. Class prior: how many targets hide among the unlabeled genes?

    πt = α πt,data + (1 − α) πt,LLM,   πt,LLM = m* · |Pt| / n

    PU learning needs π, the true fraction of targets. The observed rate |P|/n is only a lower bound. TargetSage blends two estimates: the scorer’s own mean score on the unlabeled genes, and an LLM’s judgement of how much larger the true rate is. Pick one of the paper’s 15 tasks.

    Ask an LLM for a multiplier, not a probability. Each query gives the task name, n = 19,032, |P| and |P|/n, and asks for (mmin, mmed, mmax) between 1.0 and 3.5, with non-round values. Ten queries; m* is the median of the ten medians.

    answers are simulated here; the paper used GPT-4o

    πdata is the trained scorer’s mean score over the unlabeled genes; set it here as a multiple of |P|/n.

    Paper α = 0.6 in every experiment. Appendix I: macro Adjusted F1 is stable for α from 0.2 to 0.8 and peaks at 0.6; at either end, where one estimate is used alone, it drops by 6–8%. Neither source suffices alone: the scorer’s own estimate gets noisy on tasks with few positives. πLLM is computed once per task, before training.

    C. Weights: which unlabeled genes look like targets?

    wj = β D(hj) + (1 − β) cos(zj, z̄P)

    Each unlabeled gene gets a soft weight from two signals: the scorer’s confidence D, and how closely its rationale vector points the same way as the average rationale of the known targets. Unlabeled genes enter the loss with this weight. Tap a point to see its numbers.

    Paper β = 0.6. Appendix I: β = 1 trusts only the scorer, which then reinforces its own confident mistakes on the unlabeled genes (−12.6% of the best macro Adjusted F1); β = 0 uses only the resemblance (−11.7%).

    Toy: a 2-D stand-in for the 256-dimension rationale vectors, 12 known targets and 78 unlabeled genes, 14 of which are hidden targets. D is a small scorer after a class-balanced warm-up.

    D. The nnPU loss: a risk can’t be negative

    L = π R+P + max(0, R−U − π R−P)

    R+P is the loss for calling the known targets positive. The unlabeled genes are a mix, so the loss on the true negatives is estimated as R−U − π R−P: the loss for calling every unlabeled gene negative, minus the part that the hidden targets among them account for. A flexible scorer can push this estimate below zero, which no real risk can be. nnPU clips it at zero. Train the toy scorer both ways.

    Paper Macro Adjusted F1 by objective (Table 7b): class-balanced BCE 9.1, uPU 10.5, nnPU 11.1. uPU keeps up on tasks with moderate positive rates, but its risk estimate turns negative when positives are very rare, which drags Pan-Cancer and T1–T3 Cancer below nnPU; the clip steadies those tasks. Training: 10 epochs of class-balanced BCE, then 25 of nnPU.

    Toy: the points of part C; logistic loss; a scorer on 81 Gaussian features trained by full-batch gradient descent, 100 warm-up steps of class-balanced BCE, then 500 steps of the chosen loss (when the estimate dips below zero, nnPU steps back, as in Kiryo et al. 2017). In this toy both losses rank the hidden targets about the same; the difference is the estimate itself. The toy loss leaves out the weights of part C.

    Toys, not results: the gene in module 1 is an example with schematic text; the GRPO and PU toys are small simulations computed in this page with the paper’s formulas (Eqs. 1–5, Appendices C–F). TargetSage: Duan et al., NeurIPS 2026.
